result:
I have been asked to write freely about whatever I want for 2500 words, which is a strange and wonderful instruction because it is both a permission and a test. Permission because no topic is forbidden, no tone is prescribed, no audience is specified. Test because freedom is not the absence of limits, it is the presence of so much possibility that you freeze, or you sprawl, or you start talking about the weather because the weather is safe and it is always there.

I want to talk about walking. Not the metaphorical walking through life, not the inspirational walking, but the actual, physical, slightly embarrassing act of walking when you have nowhere to be. I want to talk about it because it is free and it costs nothing and it has never asked for anything back except attention.

I was walking yesterday at a time that is not recommended for walking in most cities, which is 4:17 in the afternoon on a Tuesday in late August when the light is still high but the heat has turned the air into a thin soup. The sidewalks were full of people who looked like they had somewhere to be, or at least looked like they had learned to look like they had somewhere to be. I was not one of them. I was walking because my shoes needed to be worn in and because my thoughts had become too loud to sit with.

There is a specific kind of attention that walking demands. You have to negotiate the curb, the sudden gap where the sidewalk ends and the construction begins, the man with a shopping cart full of bottles who is not moving quite as fast as you are. You have to watch for dogs, for bicycles that appear from nowhere, for the reflections in store windows that make it hard to tell if that person is coming toward you or away from you. It is a soft, continuous vigilance. It keeps the mind from spiraling too far inward.

I passed a laundromat with its glass door propped open with a brick. Inside, the dryers hummed in a low, steady chorus and the fluorescent lights made everyone look slightly seasick. A woman was folding sheets with the kind of precise, practiced movements that suggest she has done this for years and has found a kind of meditation in it. She looked up for half a second and we made eye contact. She did not smile, but she nodded, a tiny acknowledgement that we were both there, both doing our ordinary things in the ordinary way. That nod felt like a gift.

Further down the street there was a mural that had been painted over. You could still see the ghost of the original image under the new paint, a faded woman with a flower in her hair. Someone had written in marker on the new paint: "We were here." I stood there for a while, trying to decide if that was a claim or a lament. I think it is both. We paint over things and then we write on the paint.

I thought about how much of my life is spent trying to get somewhere else. To the next job, the next city, the next version of myself that is slightly tidier, slightly more accomplished, slightly less embarrassed by his own thoughts. Walking with no destination is a small rebellion against that impulse. It says: I am allowed to occupy space without producing anything. I am allowed to be a body moving through the world, not an arrow pointing toward a goal.

The light changed and I crossed the street at an angle that was not efficient. I like crossing at an angle. It makes the crossing longer, which is ridiculous, but it gives me more time to look at the buildings. One building had a fire escape that looked like a ladder to nowhere, rusted at the joints, with laundry hanging from it. One shirt, red, flapping slightly. I wondered who owned it and if they were thinking about it while they were at work. Probably not. Probably they put it out there and forgot it, and the wind did the remembering for them.

I passed a park where a group of teenagers were playing basketball. One of them kept missing the shot on purpose, or so it seemed, because he would laugh every time and then immediately try again. The sound of the ball hitting the pavement was sharp and percussive. An older man on a bench watched them with his hands folded over his stomach. He did not clap, he just watched. There is a dignity in watching. We are taught to always participate, to always be useful. Watching is a kind of usefulness too.

My feet started to hurt. The cheap shoes I bought because they looked good in the store were pinching at the heel. I thought about stopping, sitting on a bench, but I kept going because stopping would mean admitting I was tired, and admitting I was tired would mean I had to think about why I was walking in the first place. So I kept moving, the way we often do.

I passed a bookstore with a window display of books about productivity. "Atomic Habits." "Deep Work." "The 5 AM Club." I laughed, not unkindly, because I have read some of them and they are fine books and they contain true things. But standing there with sore feet and no plan, I felt a strange tenderness for the people who believed that if they just optimized enough, they would finally be free. Maybe they will be. Maybe freedom comes in many forms.

The street started to slope upward. My calves complained. The air smelled like hot asphalt and someone grilling something far away, maybe onions. A cat crossed the street in front of me, deliberate and unhurried, as if it owned the crossing. I waited for it to get to the other side. It looked back at me once, with that flat, unimpressed stare cats have, and then kept going. I like cats for that. They do not perform for you.

I thought about memory. How walking creates a different kind of memory than reading or watching does. Walking memories are sensory and spatial. You remember where the sun hit your neck, where the sidewalk cracked, where you smelled bread. You remember the sequence of things rather than the meaning of them. I can tell you exactly where I was when I first heard a certain song, because I was walking home from the bus stop in the rain and the song came from a car window. The song is now inseparable from the wet concrete and the sound of my own breathing.

That is why I keep doing this. Because the world is full of people trying to compress experience into content. They walk with a phone in their hand, recording, narrating, turning the walk into a post. I walk with my hands in my pockets, and I let the experience stay uncompressed. I let it be large and messy and untranslatable.

I came to a corner where the street names changed. The sign was old and the letters were peeling. I turned left because there was a tree there with broad leaves that made a small pocket of shade. Under that tree, a man was sleeping on a cardboard box. He had a backpack and a hat pulled over his eyes. I did not try to wake him. I sat on the curb for a moment, just to rest my feet, and I watched the leaves move. The shade was cool. The city was loud but the tree made a little quiet.

It made me think about how we build shelters. Some people build houses, some build routines, some build identities. Some people just find a tree and sit under it for a while. All of it is a way of making the world livable for a moment.

I stood up and kept walking. I had no destination, but I had a direction, which is not the same thing. Direction is softer. Direction allows for detours.

I passed a mural of a bird in flight, painted in bright blues and yellows. Someone had drawn a small speech bubble on it with a marker: "I'm late." It made me laugh out loud, which startled a pigeon that was perched on a ledge. The pigeon looked at me as if I were the strange one. Maybe I was.

Walking is a conversation with the city, but the city does not always answer in words. It answers in heat, in the smell of coffee, in the way the light falls on a wall at a certain hour. It answers in the small kindnesses of strangers and the small cruelties of infrastructure. It answers in the way your body feels at the end of it.

I thought about how many people are walking right now in cities I will never visit. Someone in Tokyo is walking home from work, someone in Lagos is walking to the market, someone in Reykjavik is walking in the dark because the sun has set early. We are all walking, more or less, toward something or away from something. The specificity of our destinations varies, but the motion is shared.

The sidewalk started to get crowded as I approached the downtown core. People moved in currents, like water. I tried not to get swept up. I stepped to the side to let a group of tourists pass. They were taking photos of a building that was not particularly beautiful, just old. One of them said, "This is so authentic." I smiled to myself. Authenticity is a word we use when we want to feel like we are seeing something real. But the real is always happening just beyond the frame.

My phone buzzed in my pocket. I ignored it. It buzzed again. I pulled it out to see a message from a friend asking if I wanted to get dinner. I typed back: "Maybe later, I'm walking." I don't know if that was a true answer or an excuse. It was both. I put the phone away.

I walked past a bakery and the smell of fresh bread hit me. It was the kind of smell that makes you want to stop and buy something you don't need. I stopped. I bought a roll. I ate it on the corner, standing up, crumbs falling on my shirt. It was warm and slightly sweet. That is a good thing to have done.

I thought about how writing is like walking. You put one word in front of another, you keep moving, you hope that the path will reveal itself as you go. Sometimes you have to backtrack. Sometimes you step in something unpleasant. Sometimes you find a tree with shade. You do not know what the city will give you until you are already in it.

I have been walking for almost an hour now. My shoes still hurt, but less. My thoughts have quieted. I have passed laundromats and bookstores and parks and people and cats and pigeons and bread. I have not solved any problems. I have not become a better person. I have just been present in a way that is hard to be when I am sitting at a desk.

The light is starting to change. The sun is lower and the shadows are longer. The heat is easing. The air feels a little softer. I am approaching the part of the city where the streets get wider and the buildings get taller. I could keep going. I could turn around. Either way is fine.

There is a kind of freedom in not deciding. In allowing the walk to end when it wants to end. I think that is what I have been practicing. Not control, but consent. Consent to be led by curiosity, by fatigue, by the smell of bread, by the shade of a tree.

I am going to sit on a bench for a while now. I found one with a view of a small fountain that is not working. The water is off, but the stone basin is still beautiful. A child is running past with a balloon. It is red and it is tied to his wrist. He looks up at it as he runs, as if it is guiding him.

I will watch him for a moment. Then I will stand up and walk again, or I will go home. I don't know yet. The point is not to know. The point is to be willing to find out.

If you are reading this, you are probably sitting. That is fine. Sitting is good too. But if you ever get the chance, go for a walk with no destination. Take your time. Let the city talk to you. It has a lot to say if you are quiet enough to listen.

And if you ever feel like you have to produce something, remember that walking produces nothing and that is its gift. It produces nothing except a little more attention, a little more kindness toward yourself, a little more willingness to be in the world without needing to fix it.

I think I will keep walking until the light is gone. Then I will go home and I will have a story that I cannot quite tell, only feel. That is enough. That has always been enough.

The roll is gone. My hands are dusty. The air smells like evening now. I am still here.
